text.p: The following is a first reaction to Belgium's 1997 budget from a number of Belgian analysts:

Peter Praet, Chief Economist, Generale Bank: "It's a patchwork budget". The three percent Maastricht deficit target "will be realised" given the government's special powers. But Praet says he is "very disappointed" with the "negative signal" sent by the government's failure to address long-term structural reform of public sector pensions. "It's a problem of long-term economic sustainability," says Praet.
"My judgement of the budget is not on the three percent deficit target, but on the need to address the pension problem - here I'm very disappointed."

"Reform is at least beginning in private sector pensions, but little is being done in the public sector. This is one of the worst messages from the government", says Praet. "The market believes the deficit target will be met, but the government has not proved its capacity to undertake long-term structural reform."
Kristin Vandenbergen, BBL economist, said the budget was "patched together" and was "largely as expected".

"The room for manoeuvre was limited," she said. "The government couldn't raise the fiscal pressure on labour, as it's already relatively high in Belgium, and needed to look elsewhere. That it chose indirect taxes was largely expected."
"Reform of the social security system has certainly been limited. While there are some breakthroughs, it's hardly a big bang."
Vandenbergen said the market already expected Belgium to reach the three percent Maastricht budget deficit criterion.

Sylviane Delcuve at Generale Bank said the 1997 budget was better than 1996's since it contained more spending cuts and longer-lasting (austerity) measures, with an impact until at least the year 2000 or even 2005. Savings will be made on interest payments on state debt.
She said the government had taken a step in the right direction.
"This is about the first budget which deals with the problem of pensions," she said.

Commenting on the bond market's likely reaction to the budget measures, she expected the yield spread between benchmark 10-year state bonds in Belgium and Germany to narrow. She saw it stabilising at between zero and 10 basis points, noting that, compared with France, for instance, currency stability in Belgium was much better. Christer Lindholm at JP Morgan in Brussels said the budget was pretty cautious, noting this was to be expected in view of the likely resistance from unions to drastic spending cuts, particularly in social security. He said the budget was "certainly good enough" to get Belgium into monetary union.

He noted the actual pace at which the government had been reducing Belgium's huge state debt would qualify it for entry into EMU "as the progress is in the right direction. There is a dynamic in debt reduction, but there is still a long way to go. That was known at the time of the Maastricht Treaty."
Lindholm said: "If Belgium continues its efforts at consolidation it will certainly be in the monetary union."

Jean-Francois Mercier at Salomon Brothers in London said there was certainly an attempt at restraint in the budget as far as long-term problems in the spending area were concerned. "Admittedly measures are being taken."
On market reaction he said: "At the moment investors are pretty much discounting Belgium entering EMU. There is still a risk, so you require a little bit of a risk premium."
